newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Court ruling opens Bogota telephone market.
newsitem.headline: Court ruling opens Bogota telephone market.

text.p: A high court ruled Tuesday that the Colombian government had no business preventing Bogota's local telephone company from offering national and international long distance service, court sources said.

The landmark ruling, handed down by Bogota's Superior Court, would effectively end the longstanding monopoly state-run Empresa Colombiana de Telecomunicaciones (Telecom) has enjoyed over long distance service in the Colombian capital.

Court sources said the ruling specifically favors the municipally-owned Empresa de Telecomunicaciones de Santa Fe de Bogota (ETB), the Bogota telephone company. But it could have a spillover effect on other local and international carriers, since it set a precedent as to how Telecom's lion's share of Colombia's telephone market should be broken up.

Most importantly, according to ETB manager Sergio Regeros, the court ruling calls for "equal opportunities and egual conditions" by stipulating the government's Telecommunications Regulatory Commission has no right to charge ETB any fee for its entry into the long distance telephone market.
According to Regeros, who spoke in an interview with the Radionet news program, the court ruled that no fees could be imposed on ETB because none were ever payed by Telecom.
The government is expected to appeal the ruling, which could cause serious unrest in Telecom's powerful labor union.

But if it failed to win its case, the government could face the loss of millions of dollars in revenues from the planned breakup of Telecom's nationwide monopoly later this year and the sale of operating concesssions to foreign carriers.

Regeros described the court ruling as a "win-win" situation, since the opening of Bogota's long distance market would allow ETB to win a fast-growing share of the capital's lucrative long distance market by offering rates that he said would come in at about 20 percent less than those currently offered by Telecom.
"There's no valid reason to prevent the ETB from competing in the long distance market," he said.
Regeros conceded that ETB was likely to be in the market for a "strategic investor" or foreign carrier to help it provide fast and efficient long distance service.
He also said the court ruling gave the government three months before ETB would actually be able to start providing international service.
